data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is indefensible on Popper's own terms and smuggles induction back in by implicitly asserting that past performance is a reliable guide to future reliability, reducing the methodology to psychological habit rather than logical rationality.","counterconditions":[{"case":"refuted if a coherent account can be provided where preferring a better-corroborated theory is justified solely as a method to maximize the severity of future tests without any assumption that the theory will actually succeed or remain unfalsified in the future","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if Popper explicitly distinguished 'corroboration' as a report of past performance versus 'probability' as a prediction of future frequency in a way that validates action without inductive assumptions","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if it can be demonstrated that Popper explicitly justified the preference for better-corroborated theories in practical decisions solely on the grounds of maximizing testability and information content, without invoking any expectation of future success based on past performance","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By advising scientists to 'prefer' the better-corroborated theory for action, Popper implicitly relies on the principle that nature is uniform or that successful methods tend to remain successful, which contradicts his explicit rejection of induction; acting on corroboration requires an inductive leap that semantic distinctions between 'corroboration' and 'probability' cannot mask.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
